title: Net FDI Into India Rises 44% in April-August as Repatriation Cools
excerpt: Net FDI reached roughly $5.7 billion in April-August on gross inflows of about $43.8 billion, with the US the largest source and services leading sectors, RBI data showed.
body:
• Net foreign direct investment into India rose about 44% year on year in April-August, to roughly $5.7 billion from $3.96 billion a year earlier, RBI data showed.
  • Gross FDI inflows stayed strong at about $43.8 billion over the period, with equity inflows of about $24.8 billion in April-August.
  • The United States was the largest source country in the latest monthly data, ahead of Singapore, Mauritius and the UAE; services led sector inflows, followed by trading, computer services and telecom.
  • Repatriation and outward FDI by Indian firms remain the swing factors: gross inflows are robust, but net FDI depends on how much profit and capital leaves.

Net foreign direct investment into India rose about 44% year on year in the first five months of the financial year, RBI data showed, as strong gross inflows outpaced the repatriation and outward investment that have kept India's net FDI number subdued in recent years.

Net FDI for April-August came to roughly $5.7 billion, up from $3.96 billion in the same period a year earlier, according to the Reserve Bank of India's figures reported by The New Indian Express and Business Standard. Gross inflows were about $43.8 billion across the period, with equity inflows of roughly $24.8 billion in April-August alone. In the latest monthly detail, gross FDI of about $6.6 billion in a single month came with net FDI of about $5.9 billion, helped by lower repatriation and more moderate outward investment by Indian companies.

Where the money comes from — and goes

The United States was the largest source of FDI in the latest data, narrowly ahead of Singapore, followed by Mauritius and the UAE — a ranking that underscores how much of India's "Singapore" and "Mauritius" money is ultimately global capital routed through treaty jurisdictions. By sector, services drew the largest share of equity inflows, followed by trading, computer software and hardware, and telecommunications. Maharashtra continues to receive the largest state share of inflows.

The net figure is the one policymakers watch, because it nets off two large outflows: foreign investors repatriating profits and selling stakes, and Indian companies investing abroad. Both have grown as Indian firms globalise and as earlier FDI vintages mature into exits. That is why gross inflows can set records while net FDI looks modest — and why a month of lower repatriation, as in the latest data, moves the net line sharply.

Why it matters beyond the headline

FDI is the most stable component of India's external financing: unlike portfolio flows, it does not reverse in a risk-off week, and it funds the current account deficit without adding debt. A sustained rise in net FDI eases pressure on the rupee at a moment when oil above $100 is widening the import bill. For diaspora investors, the composition matters too — US-source FDI and services-led inflows track the same technology and GCC (global capability centre) expansion that employs much of the Indian-American professional class's extended networks in India.

What to watch

The RBI's monthly bulletin will show whether the April-August pace holds through the festival quarter, and whether repatriation — the volatile term in the equation — stays low. Analysts will also watch the manufacturing share of inflows, the test of whether production-linked incentives are converting announcements into factories or whether services continue to dominate India's FDI story.
